sections.h2: What does the La Paz County Recorder's Office do?
sections.html:
The La Paz County Recorder's Office records and keeps every document presented for the public record, including real property transactions, mortgages, family trusts, tax liens, mining notices, survey maps and military discharges. Parker is the county seat, and the office also keeps the voter registration rolls and handles early voting.

Records are preserved on microfilm to archival standards. Images of recorded documents from 1983 to the present can be viewed and printed online, and a public workstation is available in the office. The office accepts documents by mail, in person, and through electronic recording by a trusted submitter. The county's phone number for the Recorder is 928-669-6136, and La Paz County's website lists a Recorded Document Search page and a Forms page for the office.

sections.h2: What are the rules for recording a document in La Paz County?
sections.html:
The document must be on paper and meet the layout rules the county publishes on its Document Recording Information page. A document that fails the state requirements is returned unrecorded, and so is a document sent without the correct fees. The Recorder's Office cannot help you prepare a document.

ItemLa Paz County ruleSource
Paper size8.5 inches wide, no shorter than 11 and no longer than 14 inchesLa Paz County Recorder
First page top margin2 inches; the left 3.5 inches holds the return name and address, the right 3.5 inches is reserved for the RecorderLa Paz County Recorder; A.R.S. 11-480
Other marginsAt least 1/2 inchLa Paz County Recorder
Print10-point type or larger; black and white, except blue ink signatures or color notary stampsLa Paz County Recorder
TitleA title on the first pageLa Paz County Recorder; A.R.S. 11-480
SignaturesOriginal ink signaturesLa Paz County Recorder
Amendments or releasesState the date and instrument number of the document being modifiedLa Paz County Recorder

For the full list, the county points to A.R.S. 11-480. Once a document is accepted, the office indexes it so it can be found later and returns the original to the address typed on it, or hands it back at the counter for walk-in filers.

sections.h2: Does a La Paz County deed need an Affidavit of Property Value?
sections.html:
Yes, unless the deed is exempt. A.R.S. 11-1133 requires a deed that evidences a transfer of title to carry an affidavit completed by the buyer and the seller, or their agents, on a form the Arizona Department of Revenue approves. The recorder must refuse to record a deed that lacks a complete affidavit and has no exemption notation.

The La Paz County Forms page offers the Affidavit of Property Value, a list of exempt codes, the fee schedule PDF and a recording cover sheet. The county's FAQ says every property sale needs a completed affidavit or an exemption number, and it refers questions to the Arizona Department of Revenue at 602-716-6843.

  • Exempt transfers under A.R.S. 11-1134 include a deed of gift, a quitclaim deed given for no money, a conveyance under a court order, and a deed that confirms or corrects an earlier recorded deed.
  • Transfers for nominal consideration between spouses, between parents and children, between grandparents and grandchildren, and between siblings also qualify.
  • A trustee's deed under a power of sale, a transfer into or out of a trust for nominal consideration, and a transfer to create joint tenancy with right of survivorship are on the list as well.
  • An exempt deed must note the specific exemption on its face at the time of recording.

sections.h2: How much does the La Paz County Recorder charge?
sections.html:
Arizona law sets the base fee at $30 per recorded instrument, or $15 when a government body is a party and asks for the recording. A.R.S. 11-475 says those amounts include the charge under section 11-475.01.

Copies cost $1 for each page, according to the county's FAQ, and statute adds $3 for the recorder's certificate and seal on a certified copy. If you mail a request, the county asks for a self-addressed stamped envelope and the instrument number. The county's FAQ sends fee questions to the posted fee schedule or to the office at 928-669-6136.

A package that arrives short is returned unrecorded. Ask your title company to confirm the exact amount with the Recorder before the deed goes out, and keep the amount on the settlement statement.

sections.h2: Is there a transfer tax when you record a deed in La Paz County?
sections.html:
Article 9, Section 24 of the Arizona Constitution bars the state, counties, cities and districts from imposing any new tax, fee, stamp requirement or other assessment on the act of selling or transferring real property. Charges that already existed on December 31, 2007 are not covered by that rule.

For a seller, the practical question is which charges appear on the closing statement. The recording fee is one of them. The affidavit is a reporting form that the county assessor and the Department of Revenue use to track sales. Ask the title company to itemize everything tied to recording so you can compare it against the county fee schedule.

sections.h2: How can you find a recorded document in La Paz County?
sections.html:
Search the document images online, or ask a title company to run a search. The county's FAQ gives specific routes for common needs:

  • To find a sale price, search the document images and choose the document type affidavit of property value.
  • To find prior owners, search the grantor and grantee name index, or ask a title company for a title search.
  • To find an owner's name for a parcel, call the County Assessor at 928-669-6165.
  • To see a subdivision plat, request it from the Recorder in person or by mail, and have the map book and page number from the deed ready.

A certified or plain copy of a recorded document can be requested by instrument number, in person or by mail.

sections.h2: What is La Paz County like for people selling a house?
sections.html:
La Paz County was established on January 1, 1983, when voters separated the northern part of Yuma County, and it is the only Arizona county created after statehood. It covers 4,514 square miles in western Arizona along the Colorado River. Parker is the county seat. The incorporated places are Parker and Quartzsite, and the Colorado River Indian Reservation lies in the western part of the county.

The county describes tourism and agriculture as its leading industries. Parker's riverfront draws boaters on the 16.5-mile Parker Strip, and Quartzsite draws more than a million visitors a year to its winter gem and mineral shows. In the 2020 census 45.2 percent of housing units were vacant.

Census Bureau figures put the 2025 population at 16,711 and the housing stock at 13,783 units. The median owner-occupied home was valued at $135,800 for 2020 through 2024, owners live in 72.1 percent of occupied homes, and 38.6 percent of residents are 65 or older. Median household income was $49,478.

faqs.q: What is the phone number for the La Paz County Recorder?
faqs.a: The Recorder's FAQ lists 928-669-6136 for fee questions.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in La Paz County?
faqs.a: The state fee is $30 per instrument under A.R.S. 11-475, or $15 when a government body requests recording. Check the county's fee schedule PDF before mailing, because documents sent with incorrect fees are returned unrecorded.

faqs.q: Can I record documents electronically in La Paz County?
faqs.a: Yes, through a trusted submitter. The office also accepts documents by mail and in person.

faqs.q: How far back are La Paz County recorded documents online?
faqs.a: The county says images of recorded documents from 1983 to the present can be viewed and printed online. A public workstation is also available in the office.

faqs.q: What happens if my document does not meet the requirements?
faqs.a: It is returned to you unrecorded. The county says documents that do not meet Arizona requirements or that lack correct fees are not accepted, and the office cannot help you prepare the document.
